name: Cake Layer
purpose: The base sponge or crumb that gives the cake its identity and provides the primary eating experience between fillings.
textureContribution: Sets the fundamental crumb — light and airy for a genoise-style sponge, dense and moist for a butter cake.
structuralRole: Bears the weight of everything stacked above it; must be sturdy enough to hold its shape once cut and stacked.
flavorImpact: Usually the dominant flavor note of the whole cake, since it makes up the largest volume of any bite.
commonMistake: Overbaking to 'play it safe' — a dry sponge can't be rescued by syrup alone and will taste dense and cottony no matter what's layered around it.
proTip: Bake layers a day ahead and chill them wrapped in plastic — cold cake torts and stacks far more cleanly than a same-day warm layer.

name: Soak / Syrup
purpose: A brushed-on liquid — simple syrup, coffee, liqueur — that keeps the sponge moist and adds a secondary flavor layer.
textureContribution: Prevents the crumb from drying out, especially important for leaner sponges with less butter or oil.
structuralRole: Minimal on its own, but oversoaking weakens the crumb and can cause layers to slump — balance matters.
flavorImpact: A concentrated flavor hit that can echo or contrast the filling — coffee syrup under a mocha filling, or citrus syrup for brightness.
commonMistake: Soaking a hot layer straight out of the oven — the syrup runs straight through instead of being absorbed evenly, leaving soggy spots and dry patches.
proTip: Brush syrup on in two thin passes, letting the first soak in before the second — one heavy pass tends to pool instead of absorbing.

name: Filling
purpose: The layer spread between cake layers — buttercream, jam, curd, ganache — adding moisture, richness, and a flavor counterpoint to the sponge.
textureContribution: Introduces contrast: creamy against crumbly, or fruity-tart against sweet, depending on what's chosen.
structuralRole: Acts as the 'glue' bonding layers together — too thin and layers can shift, too thick and it squeezes out under the weight above.
flavorImpact: Often defines the cake's identity more than the sponge itself — a vanilla sponge reads completely differently with raspberry jam versus salted caramel.
commonMistake: Spreading filling all the way to the edge — it squeezes out under the weight of the layer above and creates a messy bulge along the sides.
proTip: Pipe a thin buttercream dam around the perimeter of each layer before spreading a looser filling inside it — keeps everything contained and the sides clean.

name: Crunch Layer
purpose: An optional textural layer — praline, feuilletine, nut brittle, cookie crumble — borrowed from professional pastry construction to add contrast.
textureContribution: The only source of genuine crunch in an otherwise soft cake — a deliberate textural surprise partway through a bite.
structuralRole: Thin and rigid; needs to be sandwiched carefully so it doesn't crack the layers above it when sliced.
flavorImpact: Concentrated, often nutty or caramelized flavor in a small dose — punches above its weight relative to its thin profile.
commonMistake: Adding the crunch layer while it's still warm — it can melt into the surrounding filling and lose all of its texture by the time the cake is cut.
proTip: Freeze the crunch layer flat on a tray for 10-15 minutes before placing it — it goes in rigid and stays crisp instead of deforming under the next layer.

name: Mousse
purpose: An aerated, often gelatin- or whipped-cream-stabilized layer used in entremet-style cakes for a lighter, cloud-like eating experience.
textureContribution: The lightest texture in the whole build — airy and melting rather than dense or chewy.
structuralRole: Needs to fully set (usually chilled or frozen) before the next layer goes on, typically held in shape by a cake ring or acetate collar while setting.
flavorImpact: Delivers flavor through aroma and a lingering finish rather than immediate intensity, since whipping dilutes concentration.
commonMistake: Unmolding the ring or collar before the mousse is fully set — it slumps at the edges and loses its clean vertical sides.
proTip: Run a warm (not hot) cloth around a metal ring for a few seconds right before unmolding — it releases the mousse cleanly without melting the surface.

name: Glaze / Finish
purpose: The final exterior coating — mirror glaze, ganache pour, fondant, or frosting — that seals and presents the cake.
textureContribution: The first texture a bite encounters; can be glossy-smooth, matte, or textured depending on technique.
structuralRole: Seals in moisture and, for glazes and fondant, adds a protective shell that helps the cake hold its shape during handling and transport.
flavorImpact: The first flavor note tasted and often the most visually promised one — a glaze that doesn't match the interior flavor can feel like a mismatch.
commonMistake: Pouring a glaze over a cake straight from the fridge without a crumb coat underneath — condensation forms and the glaze slides or breaks instead of setting smooth.
proTip: Glaze at the temperature the recipe specifies, not warmer 'to make it easier to pour' — too hot and it runs thin and patchy instead of coating evenly.
